title: Roman and early Byzantine coins found in India: number of gold, silver and copper coins by issuer and century, summed from Appendix 6 of Darley (2014)
source: R. R. Darley, Indo-Byzantine Exchange, 4th to 7th Centuries: a Global History, PhD thesis, University of Birmingham, 2014 (redacted version), Appendix 6 (the data of Fig. 5.8), which lists published finds from P. J. Turner (1989), Roman Coins from India; T. Sathyamurthy (1992), A Catalogue of Roman Gold Coins; B. Subrahmanyam, G. V. Rama Krishna Rao and P. Brahma Chary (2008), Roman Gold Coins: a Treasure Trove from Penuganchiprolu; R. Krishnamurthy (2007), Late Roman Copper Coins from South India
series: issuer (emperor as in the table; 'Septimius Severus' for the table's 'Severus'; Republican, Unidentified, Various), century (pre-1st, 1st, ..., 7th: the century to which the thesis assigns the reign), metal (gold, silver, copper), coins (sum of the table's lines), entries (number of lines summed)
license: The thesis reads: 'This unpublished thesis/dissertation is copyright of the author and/or third parties ... Further distribution or reproduction in any format is prohibited without the permission of the copyright holder.' The .csv (counts summed from the thesis's table) is therefore not kept in the repository (it is listed in .gitignore); run data/fetch/darley2014_coin_finds.py to download the thesis and write it. This .json and the fetch script are kept. Whether the summed counts may be kept in the repository is a question for the author of this book.
notes: PDF SHA-256 c3400e2bb1366ae4178b72b98224fea5cbbc43c6751294d3611b457df7b74536 (pages 472-476 of the PDF, pages 67-71 of the appendices). The fetch script reads the table with pdftotext -bbox and assigns each number to the column (Gold, Silver, Copper) whose heading ends nearest to it; 173 lines of the table, 41 groups. Its sums agree with the totals in the note to Fig. 5.8 of the thesis (p. 249; quoted in india_facts, row da_totals) for the 1st-century gold (756), the pre-1st-century silver (7), the 4th-century gold (1) and copper (616), the 5th-century copper (101), the 6th-century (21) and 7th-century (2) gold; they differ for the 1st-century silver (4,172 against 4,174), the pre-1st-century gold (5 against 6), the 2nd-century gold (357 against 378), the 3rd-century gold (36 against 12; the table assigns Septimius Severus, 29 coins, to the 3rd century) and the 5th-century gold (82 against 84). Chapter 9 uses the note's totals for the profile by century and the table only for the issuers of the 1st century. Darley: 'these figures are intended to be suggestive only' (p. 249). The counts are of coins reported in publications, by issuer, not of coins by date of arrival in India: a hoard buried late may hold old coins.
citation: Darley, R. R. (2014), Indo-Byzantine Exchange, 4th to 7th Centuries: a Global History, PhD thesis, University of Birmingham, Appendix 6
